abstract.t: This document specifies the Agent Discovery and Delegation Protocol (ADDP), an experimental protocol for software agents that act for a user on the Web. It lets an agent find resources published by Web origins, such as product offers, through indexes; check what an index says about a resource against the origin that published it; and carry out a narrow set of actions within limits the user approved. ADDP defines a manifest at a well-known location, a resource representation, a snapshot and change feed, a small typed query language for indexes, and the records indexes return. An optional runtime profile states what an agent must check before an action with side effects, how it recovers when the outcome of such an action is unknown, and what it shows to a language model. ADDP does not define an authorization protocol, a payment protocol, or a model tool interface.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Software agents that act for people on the Web, often driven by a language model, mostly work in one of two ways today. They read pages built for humans, or they call tools that one site exposes. Neither gives an agent a way to answer three questions that come up in almost any task that spans more than one site: where can this thing be found, is what I was told about it still true, and am I allowed to act on it within the limits the user set.

Parts of this are covered by existing work, which ADDP reuses rather than replaces (). The Universal Commerce Protocol lets a business describe its services at /.well-known/ucp and defines catalog search for that business. Agentic Resource Discovery and A2A agent cards let agents find tools, APIs and other agents. OAuth 2.0 covers authorization.
Two things appear to be missing, and this document is an experiment to find out whether they are worth standardizing:

ol.li: A feed and query contract that lets an index collect resources, such as offers, from many publishers with defined consistency, and answer structured queries over them with defined semantics. Without it, two indexes given the same data can return different answers and neither is wrong.
A stated set of checks that separates what a model proposes from what an agent actually does. Without it, "the model decided to buy" cannot be told apart from "the user authorized a purchase".

section.t: Despite its name, ADDP is not a protocol for discovering agents. The agent does the discovering: it discovers resources, and the user delegates actions on them to it.

section.name: Scope
section.t: In scope:

ul.li: Publisher metadata at a well-known URI.
Resource representation and resolution at the publisher.
Snapshot and change feeds from publishers to indexes.
A query and result format for indexes.
Capability documents that name an execution protocol.
An optional profile for agents that perform actions with side effects ().
Rules for what such an agent shows to a language model ().

section.t: Out of scope:

ul.li: Discovery of agents, tools and APIs.
An interface by which a model calls tools.
Authentication and authorization protocols.
Payment protocols.
Relevance ranking. Indexes filter; agents rank.
A universal vocabulary for products, flights, or other domains.
Replacing UCP for businesses that already implement it ().

section.name: What the Experiment Should Show
section.t: This document is intended for Experimental status. The experiment succeeds if the following can be shown. If they cannot, the useful parts of ADDP should become profiles of existing protocols instead.

ol.li: Two independent index implementations that consume the same feeds return the same result sets for the same queries.
Resolution () catches index claims that are stale often enough to justify its cost.
At least one execution protocol in real use can meet the requirements in . Only a sandbox binding exists today ().
The views in reduce the tokens a model consumes per completed task without lowering the rate at which tasks are completed correctly, measured on named models.

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: An origin that publishes resources and, optionally, a feed.
A service that collects resources from publishers and answers queries about them.
The part of an agent that performs discovery and, if it implements , actions. It holds credentials and enforces the user's limits. The user trusts it.
A language model that reads data and proposes what to do next. The runtime treats its output as untrusted input.
Something a publisher describes, identified by a resource reference. In this document a resource is an item such as an offer, not a tool or an agent.
The triple (publisher, namespace, id) defined in .
A named set of rules that gives the facts of a resource a meaning and says which query predicates apply to them ().
A named set of rules for one kind of action, used by capability documents and intents ().
A statement made by a publisher or an index. Claims are inputs to decisions; they are never authorization.
An index's claim about a resource, returned in answer to a query.
A condition the user requires, such as a maximum price. A resource that does not demonstrably meet a hard constraint does not meet it.
A document that describes an operation on a resource and names the protocol that performs it.
Code in the runtime, installed by the runtime's operator, that performs one operation of one version of one execution protocol.
Objects of the runtime profile, defined in .

section.name: Protocol Overview

figure.name: Message Flow
figure.artwork: Publisher Index Runtime Model | | | | |<-- manifest, feed-| (pull) | | | |<----- query ------| | | |--- candidates --->| | | | |---- view ------>| | | |<-- proposal ----| |<---------- resolve -------------------| | |<------ execution binding (optional) --| |

section.t: A publisher describes itself in a manifest and publishes resources, usually through a feed. An index pulls feeds and answers queries with candidates. A runtime queries one or more indexes it was configured to use, ranks the candidates itself, and shows the model a small view of them. When the model proposes to act on a candidate, the runtime first resolves the resource at its publisher and checks it again. If the runtime implements the runtime profile and the user has approved the action, the runtime performs it through an execution binding.

Authority to act comes from two places only: the user's approval, which the runtime records, and the authorization that the service performing the action enforces. Nothing a publisher, an index, or a model says adds to it.

section.name: HTTP and JSON
section.t: ADDP messages are exchanged over HTTPS. HTTP methods, status codes and header fields have the meanings given in .

Every ADDP message is a JSON object that is also an I-JSON message , encoded in UTF-8 and sent with media type application/json. In particular, a receiver MUST reject a message that contains duplicate member names, invalid UTF-8, or unpaired surrogates. A receiver MUST reject a message nested more than 32 levels deep.
Members that this document defines as integers MUST be written without a fraction or an exponent and MUST be in the range 0 to 2^53-1. A receiver MUST reject 5.0 or 5e0 where an integer is required.

section.name: Versioning, Unknown Members, and Extensions
section.t: The manifest, resource, feed head, snapshot part, change list, query, query response, capability document, intent and quote each have a member version whose value is "0.1". A receiver MUST reject other values. These objects, and only these, may also carry extensions and critical_extensions.

Objects are closed. A receiver MUST reject a message with a member this document does not define, with two exceptions. The content of facts is defined by the resource profile (). The member extensions is an object whose member names are absolute URIs without a fragment, and whose values are not constrained here.

The member critical_extensions is an array of extension URIs. A receiver MUST reject a message that lists an extension it does not implement. A receiver MAY ignore extensions that are not listed as critical. An extension MUST NOT change the identity of a resource, relax a constraint, or grant authority, whether or not it is critical.

section.name: Origins and URLs
section.t: An origin is serialized as in : scheme https, the host in lower case, and the port only if it is not 443. Host names MUST be ASCII; internationalized names appear in A-label form.

Every URL in an ADDP message that a client fetches MUST be an absolute https URL of at most 512 characters, without user information and without a fragment. Resource types and extension names are absolute URIs that are compared but not fetched. Receivers compare URLs and URIs as strings and MUST NOT normalize them before comparison. Two URLs that differ only in case, percent-encoding or a trailing slash are different URLs.

section.name: Resource References
section.t: A resource reference is an object with three members, all required:

dl.dd: The serialized origin of the publisher.
"addp" or "ucp.catalog".

For "addp", an https URL whose origin is publisher; the resource is resolved by fetching it. For "ucp.catalog", a UCP catalog product or variant ID issued by publisher; the resource is resolved through the adapter in .

section.t: Two references are equal when all three members are equal as strings. A reference does not identify the same thing at another publisher, even if the id happens to be the same.

section.name: Time and Money
section.t: Timestamps are date-time values in UTC of the form YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ, optionally with a decimal fraction of one to nine digits before the Z. A receiver MUST reject other forms, including numeric UTC offsets.

A monetary amount is an object with amount_minor, an integer number of minor units, and currency, an ISO 4217 alphabetic code . EUR 333.99 is {"amount_minor": 33399, "currency": "EUR"}. A receiver MUST reject an amount in a currency whose minor-unit exponent it does not know. Amounts in different currencies are never equal and never compare as greater or smaller; a comparison between them fails. ADDP defines no conversion between currencies.

section.name: Size Limits
section.t: A message MUST NOT exceed 1 MiB after content decoding. Arrays have the maximum lengths given where they are defined. A receiver MUST reject a message that exceeds a limit and MUST enforce the size limit while decoding, not after.

section.name: Errors
section.t: Errors are problem details sent with media type application/problem+json. The type member is about:blank, title is the reason phrase registered for the status code, and an extension member code carries one of the values below. A detail member is optional. It MUST NOT contain credentials or internal state, and receivers MUST treat it as untrusted text for display only.

tr.td: Origin mismatch, disallowed address, or missing authority
The resource or object does not exist
Epoch, watermark, revision or quote does not match
Cursor, snapshot or change history no longer available
A size or count limit was exceeded
Wrong media type or content coding
A predicate, operator, field or mode is not supported
The profile or execution binding is not supported
A critical extension is not implemented
A hard constraint is not met

section.t: An example is in .

section.name: Fetching
section.t: Discovery requests are the requests a client makes to fetch manifests, feeds, resources and capability documents, and to query public indexes. The following applies to them.

ul.li: A client MUST NOT send cookies, an Authorization header, a client certificate, or any other per-user identifier.

A client MUST resolve the host name itself and MUST NOT connect if any resolved address is not globally routable, including loopback, private, link-local and unique local addresses and IPv4-mapped forms of them. It MUST connect to an address it checked, so that a second DNS answer cannot redirect the connection, and it MUST still validate the TLS certificate against the host name in the URL.
A client MUST NOT follow a redirect to another origin and MUST NOT follow more than three redirects. It MUST apply the address check again on each hop.
A client MUST accept only the content codings identity and gzip.

section.t: A runtime operator MAY configure specific private publishers, for example inside an organization. Such configuration is outside this document.

section.name: Manifest
section.t: A publisher MAY publish a manifest at /.well-known/addp . A client MAY also learn a manifest URL through configuration.

dl.dd: "0.1". Required.
"addp". Required.
The publisher's origin. Required. It MUST equal the origin the manifest was fetched from; a client MUST reject the manifest otherwise.
The resource profiles of the publisher's resources, 1 to 8 entries. Required.
URL of the feed head (). Optional.
URLs of capability documents, at most 32, possibly none. Required.
Present if the origin also operates an index. An object with endpoint (URL), profiles, text_modes (["lexical"]) and max_limit (1 to 100). Optional.

section.t: Every URL in a manifest MUST have the manifest's origin. Hosting on another origin would need an explicit delegation mechanism, which this version does not define; redirects do not stand in for one.
A manifest describes what a publisher offers. It does not authorize anything. An example is in .
A publisher that already publishes a UCP profile at /.well-known/ucp does not need an ADDP manifest. A runtime can read its catalog through the adapter in .

section.name: Representation

dl.dd: The resource reference.
An absolute URI naming the kind of thing, for example https://schema.org/Offer .
One of the resource profiles in .

An opaque string that changes whenever the representation changes, or null. It is compared only for equality. It MUST NOT be null for namespace "addp". It is null when an adapter maps a source that has no revisions.
An object whose members are defined by the resource profile, at most 64 members.
URLs of capability documents that apply to this resource, at most 32. They MUST have the publisher's origin.
A timestamp until which the publisher states that the facts remain accurate, or null if it makes no such statement.

section.t: All members are required. extensions and critical_extensions are permitted. An example is in .

section.name: Resolution
section.t: For namespace "addp", a client resolves a reference by sending a discovery request () for GET on id with Accept: application/json. The response is a resource. Its ref MUST equal the requested reference; a client MUST reject it otherwise. A publisher returns 404 or 410 for a resource that does not exist.
A resolved resource is what the publisher says now. It is not a reservation and not a price commitment. A price commitment, if the domain has one, comes from a quote ().

section.name: Resource Profiles
section.t: This version defines two resource profiles. A receiver MUST reject a resource with any other profile. How to add profiles without a new protocol version is an open issue ().

section.name: core/0.1
section.t: Any type. facts may contain name, a string of at most 512 characters. Query predicates on type and publisher apply ().

section.name: offer-search/0.1
section.t: type MUST be https://schema.org/Offer. All members of facts are optional, but unit_price_minor and currency appear together or not at all. No other members are permitted.

tr.td: Price of one unit in minor units, as offered by the publisher. It never includes shipping. This profile does not say whether it includes tax.
Colour as stated by the publisher; free text
GTIN, 8 to 14 digits, as claimed by the publisher

section.t: Because unit_price_minor excludes shipping and may exclude tax, it cannot show that a purchase stays within a limit on the total. A runtime that has such a limit needs a quote ().

section.name: Feeds
section.t: A feed lets an index copy a publisher's resources and keep the copy current. It consists of a head, which points to a snapshot, and an optional list of changes that follow the snapshot. Feeds are pulled over HTTPS with discovery requests.

section.name: Head
section.t: A GET on the manifest's feed URL returns a head:

dl.dd: An opaque string. Sequence numbers are meaningful only within one epoch.
An object with id; through, the sequence number after which the snapshot reflects the publisher's state; parts, 1 to 1024 URLs; and expires_at.
URL of the change list. Optional.

section.t: Every URL in a head MUST have the publisher's origin. An example is in .

section.name: Snapshot Parts
section.t: Each part has epoch, snapshot_id, through and resources (at most 10000). The first three MUST match the head. Together, the parts contain every resource the publisher publishes through this feed, each exactly once, as of sequence number through. Every resource MUST have the feed's origin as its publisher. A publisher MUST serve every part of a snapshot, unchanged, until the snapshot's expires_at. An example is in .

section.name: Installing a Snapshot
section.t: An index MUST fetch and validate all parts of a snapshot before expires_at, and only then replace what it holds for that publisher. The replacement MUST be atomic for readers: a query sees either the old set or the new set. If any part is missing or invalid, the index keeps the old set. Parts of different snapshots MUST NOT be combined.
Resources absent from an installed snapshot are deleted. Within one epoch, an index MUST NOT install a snapshot whose through is lower than that of the snapshot or changes it already holds.

section.name: Changes
section.t: A client requests changes with GET on the changes URL with query parameters epoch, after (the last sequence number the client has applied) and optionally limit. The response is a change list:

dl.dd: The epoch.
Equal to after.
The last sequence number included, or from_exclusive if there are none.
At most 10000 events. Each has seq and op. An "upsert" event carries the complete new resource; a "delete" event carries the ref of the deleted resource.
True if further events existed when the response was built.

section.t: Sequence numbers are assigned by the publisher, one per change, with no gaps. The events in a response MUST have the consecutive numbers from_exclusive+1 to through. The publisher may return fewer events than limit.

An index applies a change list as follows. It MUST validate every event first and apply all of them atomically. If through is not greater than the index's watermark, the list is a replay and the index ignores it. If from_exclusive differs from the watermark, or the epoch differs, the index MUST NOT apply the list; it requests changes again from its watermark or installs a new snapshot. After applying, the watermark is through.

A publisher MUST keep every change after the through of each snapshot that has not expired. If it no longer has the changes after after, it responds with cursor_expired, and the index installs a new snapshot. If the epoch is not current, it responds with state_conflict. A 404 or 410 response for the feed or change list MUST NOT be treated as the deletion of all resources. An example is in .

section.name: Other Sources
section.t: An index MAY collect resources from sitemaps, product feeds, UCP catalogs or other sources through adapters. It MUST NOT present such data as having the consistency described in this section unless the source provides the same guarantees.

section.name: Request
section.t: A client sends a query with POST to the index's query endpoint, as application/json with no content coding. An initial query has these members:

dl.dd: The resource profile whose predicates and fields the query uses. A query with profile core/0.1 matches resources of any profile. A query with offer-search/0.1 matches only resources with that profile.
Optional. An object with mode ("lexical") and value ().
Up to 32 predicates, all of which must hold. Each has field, op and value.
Fields of facts to return ().
Page size, 1 to 100. If it exceeds the index's max_limit, the index uses max_limit.

section.t: A continuation query has only version and cursor (). An example is in .

section.name: Predicates
section.t: A predicate on unit_price_minor requires exactly one currency predicate in the same query. A resource that lacks the field, or has a value of the wrong type, does not match. in takes an array of 1 to 32 strings.

An index MUST reject a query that uses a field, operator, value or text mode it does not support, with unsupported_query. It MUST NOT drop a predicate and answer the rest of the query: a result for a weaker query presented as the result of the stronger one is a wrong answer.

section.name: Lexical Text
section.t: With mode "lexical", value is split on white space into terms. A resource matches if, for every term, the canonical caseless form of the term is a substring of the canonical caseless form of facts.name. The canonical caseless form of a string X is NFD(toCasefold(NFD(X))), as defined in Section 3.13 of . A value with no terms is rejected. Text is a filter here, not a ranking signal.

section.name: Selected Fields
section.t: select names fields of facts defined by the query's profile. The index returns those fields and also every field of facts used in a predicate, so that a client can see why a candidate matched. Selecting a field the profile does not define is rejected with unsupported_query.

section.name: Order and Pagination
section.t: Results are ordered by reference: by publisher, then namespace, then id, each compared as a sequence of Unicode code points. Indexes do not rank. A runtime that wants a ranking computes it.

All pages of one query reflect one state of the index, taken when the initial query was answered. Pages do not overlap and do not skip results. next_cursor is an opaque string, or null on the last page. A continuation query returns the next page, and repeating it returns the same page. An unknown or expired cursor is rejected with cursor_expired; the client then starts over.

An index that authenticates clients MUST bind cursors to the client and reject them from another client with forbidden. An index MAY limit the number of live cursors per client. It SHOULD NOT let the queries of one authenticated client expire the cursors of another. Unauthenticated clients cannot be told apart and share one limit.

section.name: Response
section.t: The response has version, snapshot (an opaque identifier of the index state the pages reflect), items (at most 100 candidates) and next_cursor. An example is in .

section.name: Candidates
section.t: A candidate has these members, all required:

dl.dd: As in the resource.
The revision of the resource the index holds, or null.
When the index fetched that revision, or null if unknown.
When the index stored it.
Copied from the resource.
The fields described in .
"yes", "no" or "unknown": whether the publisher paid the index to include this resource. Since results are not ranked, position cannot be bought; inclusion can.

section.t: A candidate is a claim by the index about a claim by the publisher. A runtime MUST NOT use a candidate as authorization or as the price of any action.

section.name: Resolution and Re-evaluation
section.t: Before a runtime tells the user that a candidate meets the user's hard constraints, and before any action concerning it, the runtime MUST resolve the reference at the publisher () and evaluate every hard constraint against the resolved resource. That includes the predicates and text of the query that produced the candidate, and the constraints the runtime applied itself instead of sending them to the index, whether for privacy () or because the index cannot filter on them. If any constraint does not hold, the candidate is not eligible. A runtime MUST NOT relax a constraint to keep a candidate eligible. If the user wants to relax a constraint, that is a new decision by the user.
For example, an index reports a price of EUR 329.00. The resolved resource says EUR 389.00, and the query required at most EUR 350.00. The candidate is not eligible.

section.name: Querying Several Indexes
section.t: A runtime queries a set of indexes configured by its user or operator. It MUST NOT query an index it learned about from a publisher, another index, or content shown to a model, unless the user or operator adds it to that set.

The runtime records, for each index, whether the query succeeded, failed, was rate limited or timed out. If any did not succeed, the combined result is partial, and the runtime MUST say so wherever it presents the result ().

Candidates with equal references describe the same resource. If they differ in source_revision, the runtime resolves the resource rather than picking one. Candidates with different references are different resources, even if they share a GTIN or a name; the runtime MUST NOT merge them, their prices, or any authority related to them.

section.name: Capabilities
section.t: A capability document describes an operation on a resource:

dl.dd: The URL of the document itself.
The operation profile.
A string identifying this version of the document.
Each an object with url and sha256, the lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 hash of the exact bytes of the schema document after content decoding.
Up to 16 strings describing side effects. Advisory.
An object with protocol, protocol_version, endpoint and operation.

section.t: The document's id, binding.endpoint and schema URLs MUST have the publisher's origin. An example is in .

The capability digest is the SHA-256 hash of the exact bytes of the capability document as the runtime received it, after content decoding. A runtime computes it itself and MUST NOT use a digest supplied by a publisher, an index or a quote in its place. A document whose bytes changed, even only in formatting, has a different digest.

A runtime MUST NOT perform an operation unless it has an execution binding for the exact protocol, protocol_version and operation, installed by the runtime's operator. A runtime MUST NOT download or run code offered by a publisher to perform an operation. Declared effects MUST NOT reduce the checks the runtime applies. An operation whose effects are unknown to the runtime is treated as irreversible.

section.name: Runtime Profile
section.t: This section applies to runtimes that perform actions with side effects for a user. A runtime that only discovers and presents resources need not implement it. The objects in this section are local to the runtime or exchanged with the execution binding; they are not published.

section.name: Roles
section.t: The model proposes. The runtime decides whether a proposal is within what the user approved. The service that performs the action enforces its own authorization. None of these steps may be skipped on the grounds that another has been done.

section.name: Intent
section.t: An intent records what the user approved. This document defines one operation profile for intents, sandbox-purchase/0.1, used by the sandbox binding ():

dl.dd: Identifier and revision number, starting at 1.
ref and quantity (1).
max_total, an amount, and max_count (1), the number of operations allowed.
purchase (boolean), substitution (false), recurring (false).
The digest of the capability document the user's approval covered.
End of validity.

section.t: max_total is the most the merchant may charge for the whole intent, as the quote's total states it. Fees charged to the payer by others, such as currency conversion fees, are not included unless the execution binding guarantees otherwise.
Rules:

ul.li: Intents are created and changed only by a path that records the user's approval. A model MUST NOT be able to create, approve or change an intent; it can only propose one.

A revision is immutable. A change creates revision n+1. A runtime MUST NOT accept a new revision while an operation for the intent is unresolved, and MUST NOT accept one whose constraints are already exceeded by recorded spending.
Permission to search does not imply permission to buy.
A runtime MUST NOT act on an intent that contains a constraint it does not understand.
Intents are not sent to publishers or indexes.

section.t: An example is in .

section.name: Quote
section.t: A quote is the service's statement of what it will charge for a specific checkout session: id, revision, session, ref, quantity, total (an amount), total_scope ("merchant_total", meaning all the merchant charges including tax and shipping), capability_digest and expires_at. How a runtime obtains a quote depends on the execution binding. An example is in .

section.name: Checks Before Execution
section.t: Before dispatching an operation, a runtime MUST:

ol.li: Confirm that the intent revision is approved, not cancelled and not expired, and that it permits the action.
Compute the digest of the capability document it is about to use and confirm that it equals the intent's capability_digest. If the document changed, the earlier approval does not cover it.
Select the execution binding installed for the document's exact protocol, protocol_version and operation, and confirm that binding.endpoint has the origin of the intent's target publisher.
Obtain a current quote, confirm that it has not expired, and confirm that its capability_digest equals the digest computed in step 2.

Confirm that the quote's reference and quantity equal the intent's target, that its currency matches max_total, and that total plus the amounts already reserved or spent for the intent does not exceed max_total.
Build the operation from the intent and the quote, not from text written by the model.

section.t: The operation carries intent_id, intent_revision, quote_id, quote_revision, session, ref, quantity, total and capability_digest. An example is in .

The runtime chooses an identifier for each operation, and the service uses it to recognize repeats. The identifier MUST contain at least 128 bits from a cryptographically secure random source, or be guaranteed unique in some other way among all runtimes that act for the same user.

section.name: Requirements on Execution Bindings
section.t: A runtime MUST NOT perform an operation through a binding without asking the user at the time, unless the service behind the binding:

ol.li: records the outcome of every operation identifier it accepts for processing, rejections included, returns that outcome for any later request with the same identifier and an identical operation, and rejects the same identifier with a different operation;

answers a status request for an identifier and an operation with the recorded outcome, with "not found" if nothing is recorded for the identifier, or with "conflict" if a different operation is recorded for it;
enforces authorization itself, independent of the runtime's checks, including expiry and revocation.

section.t: A service need not record requests it cannot attribute to a valid authorization. If it did, a third party could use up identifiers.

If a binding cannot meet these requirements, the runtime hands the action to the user. The binding documentation MUST say which component enforces each requirement. A limit on the maximum amount of a payment credential is not the same as requirement 1: it caps a charge but does not tie it to the quoted total.

section.name: Reservations
section.t: A runtime keeps a durable journal. Before dispatch it reserves the operation's total against the intent, in one atomic step with the checks in , so that two concurrent operations cannot both fit under a limit that only one fits under. A reservation is released only when it is known that the operation had no effect and never will: it was never dispatched, the service recorded a failed outcome for it (requirement 2), or the service reports a conflict (requirement 3), in which case the identifier belongs to a different operation and this one can never be accepted. A limit that must hold across several runtimes needs a component that all of them consult; separate journals do not provide it.

section.name: Outcomes and Recovery
section.t: An operation is not_started, in_progress, pending, succeeded, failed, cancelled or unknown. succeeded, failed and cancelled are final.

ul.li: If the runtime sent an operation and did not get an answer, or got an error without a recorded outcome, the outcome is unknown, not failed. The runtime MUST keep the reservation and ask the service for the status.

"Not found" does not settle the operation: the request may still be in transit. The runtime MAY send the identical operation again with the same identifier. Because of requirement 2, this either performs the operation once or returns the recorded outcome. The runtime MUST NOT send the operation under a new identifier.

Cancelling an intent stops operations not yet dispatched and releases their reservations. It does not release the reservation of an operation that may have been dispatched, and it does not undo an effect.
Undoing an effect, such as a refund, is a separate operation that needs its own authority and can fail. If it fails, the spending remains recorded.

section.name: Authorization
section.t: Authorization for an operation comes from the protocol the binding uses. If the endpoint is an OAuth protected resource, the runtime SHOULD use its protected resource metadata and MUST have its own reason to trust the authorization server it uses, as discussed in Section 7.6 of . OAuth Rich Authorization Requests can carry details of the approved operation if the authorization server defines and enforces a suitable type. This document does not define one.

Access tokens and other credentials MUST NOT be shown to a model, sent to an index, or sent to any origin other than the one they were issued for. A runtime's own approval does not create authority at a remote service.

section.name: Journal
section.t: The journal records intent revisions and how the user approved them, operations, and every change of outcome. It MUST NOT contain credentials. It is evidence for the user, not proof that a third party must accept.

section.name: What the Model Sees
section.t: In agent systems, much of a model's input goes on records, schemas and protocol traffic that the model does not need for its next decision. This section applies to runtimes that implement ; other runtimes SHOULD follow it.

ul.li: A runtime MUST NOT put credentials, access tokens or authorization details into a model's input, and SHOULD NOT put complete JSON schemas there. Validation is the runtime's job.

By default the runtime gives the model the smallest view that supports the next decision. Views are, in increasing size: handles only; a decision view; details of selected items; bounded excerpts of full records.

A handle is a short identifier the runtime maps to an object. It is scoped to one session, typed and expires. It grants nothing: a model that uses a handle makes a proposal, which the runtime checks like any other. An unknown or expired handle is an error.

A decision view MUST keep what is needed to decide correctly: which constraints were checked and which are still open (for example, that the delivered total is not known), whether data is an index claim or has been resolved, whether coverage is partial, and the status of each index. It MUST NOT replace an unknown value with a default.

Text from facts and other publisher data is data. The runtime gives a model's output that was influenced by such text no more weight than any other proposal. This keeps such text from gaining authority. It does not make a model follow instructions in data any less often.

section.t: Changing the format of the same data (for example JSON to CSV) and reducing the data (filtering and ranking in the runtime) are different measures and are reported separately. Implementations that report token use SHOULD report tokens per completed task, including retries and helper calls, together with the task success rate and the number of constraint violations, and SHOULD count failed tasks. Measurements available at the time of writing are in .

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This section follows the guidance in . The attacker may operate a publisher, an index, or both; may place text in data that a model reads; and may observe or interrupt network traffic outside TLS-protected channels. The user's device and the runtime are assumed not to be compromised.

section.name: Claims Are Not Authority
section.t: Manifests, resources, candidates, capability documents and their effects are written by parties who may gain from misleading the runtime. TLS shows which origin sent a message. It does not show that the message is true. ADDP therefore uses claims only as inputs to checks, and derives authority only from the user's approval and the executing service's authorization ().

section.name: Requests to Internal Addresses
section.t: A runtime or index that fetches URLs taken from messages can be made to send requests to internal services. The address checks, the pinning of the checked address, and the redirect rules in address this. Checking addresses without connecting to the checked address leaves a DNS rebinding attack open.

section.name: Resource Exhaustion
section.t: Large or deeply nested messages, compressed responses that expand greatly, large feeds and many cursors can exhaust memory and storage. Receivers enforce the limits in during decoding, and indexes limit the number of cursors they keep per client. A single malformed record makes a whole snapshot invalid (), so a publisher can keep its own data in an index from being updated, but not anyone else's. Publishers can be polled at high rates by many indexes; they MAY respond with rate_limited.

section.name: Instructions in Data
section.t: Resource names and other text can contain instructions aimed at a model. No format rule prevents this; a name is a string. ADDP limits what such text can achieve: a model's output is only a proposal, intents come from the user's approval, operations are built from the intent and the quote, and credentials never reach the model (). Within those limits a manipulated model can still propose a legitimate but poor option. The user's constraints bound the damage; they do not remove it.

section.name: Index Manipulation
section.t: An index can omit resources, include resources for payment, or return stale facts. Fixed ordering () removes ranking as a lever, and paid_inclusion discloses paid inclusion if the index is honest. Resolution () catches stale or false facts about resources that are returned. Omission cannot be detected from one index; querying several independent indexes reduces it.

section.name: Changing Prices
section.t: A publisher can show one price in its feed and charge another. The resolved resource and the quote are checked again before execution, and requirement 1 in makes the service reject an operation whose total differs from its quote. Together these turn a changed price into a failed operation rather than a larger charge, provided the binding meets that requirement.

section.name: Changed or Substituted Capabilities
section.t: A publisher can change a capability document after the user approved an action based on it. The runtime computes the digest of the document itself and compares it with the one in the intent (); a changed document needs new approval. A digest supplied by the publisher, for example in a quote, cannot replace this check, because the publisher controls both. The same-origin rules keep a capability from pointing execution at another origin. Execution bindings are installed by the runtime's operator, so a publisher cannot supply the code that performs its own operations.

section.name: Retries and Lost Responses
section.t: Treating a lost response as a failure and retrying under a new identifier can perform an action twice. requires the unknown state, status requests, and retries only under the same identifier. Requirement 2 in also records rejections, so a copy of a rejected request that arrives late cannot succeed. Random identifiers of at least 128 bits () keep two runtimes from choosing the same identifier by accident.

section.name: Limits Across Runtimes
section.t: A user with several devices, each with its own runtime and journal, can exceed a limit that each runtime enforces locally. Only a component all of them consult, such as the executing service or a payment provider, can enforce a shared limit.

section.name: Authorization Servers and Tokens
section.t: A publisher can name an authorization server under an attacker's control. does not define how a client decides which authorization servers to trust, and neither does this document; a runtime needs its own basis for that decision. Tokens are sent only to the origin they were issued for and never to a model or an index ().

section.name: Cursors and Handles
section.t: A cursor for a public query gives access only to results that anyone could obtain; for authenticated indexes it is bound to the client. Handles are local to a session and grant nothing, so a model that invents or reuses a handle can at most propose something the runtime then checks.

section.name: Not Addressed
section.t: This document does not protect against a merchant that takes payment and does not deliver, a compromised runtime or user device, omission by every configured index, or a model that chooses badly among options that all meet the user's constraints.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: This section follows .

ul.li: Queries tell an index what the user is looking for. A runtime SHOULD send only the predicates needed to keep the result set manageable and apply other constraints locally; they are then checked at resolution (). It MUST NOT send addresses, payment details or intent identifiers to an index.
Each additional index learns the query. This is one reason indexes are configured, not discovered.

Discovery requests carry no cookies or per-user identifiers (), so a publisher cannot link them to a user account. The publisher still learns which resources are being resolved, and can link requests by network address. A runtime MAY resolve only the candidates it is about to present.
A cursor links the pages of one query. Indexes SHOULD NOT keep cursors or query logs with client identifiers longer than needed to serve the query.
The journal contains what the user bought and when. It stays with the runtime.
The UCP adapter sends the search text and currency to the business, not the user's price limit ().

section.name: UCP Catalog Adapter
section.t: This appendix describes how a runtime reads a UCP catalog as ADDP resources. It covers only the subset the reference implementation supports, pinned to UCP version 2026-08-25, and is not a UCP implementation.

ul.li: The runtime reads the business profile at /.well-known/ucp. It requires ucp.version 2026-08-25, exactly one REST service of that version under dev.ucp.shopping whose endpoint has the business's origin, and the capabilities dev.ucp.shopping.catalog.search and dev.ucp.shopping.catalog.lookup at that version.
Search is POST {endpoint}/catalog/search with query, context.currency and pagination.limit. The runtime does not send the user's price limit; it applies hard constraints after mapping.

Each product variant becomes one resource with reference (business origin, "ucp.catalog", variant id), type https://schema.org/Offer, profile offer-search/0.1 and revision null. The variant title becomes name, price.amount and price.currency become unit_price_minor and currency, and a boolean availability.available becomes availability. Nothing maps to condition, so such resources never match a condition predicate.
Resolution is POST {endpoint}/catalog/lookup with ids containing the variant ID.
The adapter adds no feed consistency, freshness or revision guarantees that UCP does not provide.

section.t: The fixtures the tests use:

dl.dd: UCP covers business discovery, capability negotiation, catalog search and checkout for one business . The ADDP manifest and query overlap with it. ADDP adds consistency rules for feeds, a query whose semantics hold across indexes, re-evaluation at the origin, and the runtime profile. If the experiment shows that these fit into UCP, they should go there.

ACP defines a checkout API that an agent calls at a merchant, and a payment token that the merchant can use for one checkout up to a maximum amount. Its idempotency keys meet requirement 2 of , except that responses with status 5xx are not recorded and keys may expire after 24 hours. It has no status request per key; retrieving the checkout session and repeating the identical request serve that purpose while the key is kept. The request that completes a checkout carries no expected total, and the token's maximum caps the charge without fixing it, so requirement 1 is not met without an extension. ACP also proposes product feeds that merchants push to a service hosted by the agent. Like ADDP, it treats the checkout, not the feed, as authoritative.

AP2 works inside a commerce protocol and secures a purchase with signed mandates. A closed checkout mandate is bound to a checkout the merchant signed, and a payment mandate to the same checkout, which gives the exact binding that requirement 1 of asks for. Without the user present, the user signs open mandates with constraints (merchants, items and quantities, amount range, budget, number of uses, expiry) and the agent signs the closed ones; the merchant and the credential provider check them against the constraints. An intent could be expressed as open mandates, so that parties other than the runtime can enforce its limits (). AP2 leaves retries, idempotency and status requests to the commerce protocol.

ARD lets domains publish catalogs of tools, APIs, agents and skills at /.well-known/ard.json, and lets registries crawl them and answer searches that combine natural-language text with equality filters, ranked by each registry. ARD finds capabilities; ADDP finds items such as offers, with typed facts. ARD defines no change feeds, fixed result order or re-evaluation at the origin, and it stops before invocation. An ADDP index could be listed in ARD registries as an entry.

A2A publishes agent cards at the registered well-known URI agent-card.json. specifies discovery and invocation of agents, and collects requirements for agent protocols. These concern finding and calling agents, which ADDP does not do.

The Agent Web Protocol draft lets a site describe its actions for agents in one JSON file, with sensitivity, idempotency and authentication hints. It overlaps with the ADDP manifest and capability documents. It defines no feeds, index queries, re-evaluation or spending limits.

ADDP uses OAuth as is. Protected resource metadata and authorization server metadata help a runtime find authorization servers. Rich Authorization Requests and Token Exchange can express and narrow delegated authority, if a server supports them for the operation in question.

Protocols that let a model call tools, or let agents call each other, can serve as execution bindings. A capability names the exact protocol and version, and the binding documents which of the requirements in it meets.
Resource types are Schema.org URIs. The Schema.org vocabulary does not define execution semantics, which is why profiles are needed.

section.name: Sandbox Execution Binding
section.t: The reference implementation contains a binding with protocol addp-sandbox, version 0.1, operation commit. It exists to test and moves no money. Its service keeps quotes, grants and operation outcomes in one database. In one transaction it checks the grant (intent, publisher, currency, maximum amount, expiry, revocation), the quote (revision, session, reference, quantity, total, capability digest, expiry) and the operation identifier, and records the outcome, including a rejection. It answers status requests with the recorded outcome, "not found" or "conflict". It meets the four requirements of because the quote and the charge live in one database. A real payment flow spreads them over several services and has to be analyzed separately.

The tests cover a successful purchase; a repeated operation; a response lost after the service committed; a restart of the runtime; a crash after dispatch followed by a resend under the same identifier; a late copy of a rejected request; an identifier held by a different operation; a quote changed at the service; a changed capability document, including a change of formatting only; a missing execution binding; a substituted resource; two concurrent operations against one limit; an expired and a revoked grant; cancellation of a pending operation; and a failed refund.

section.name: Measurements
section.t: The companion repository contains a script that builds an index of 20 synthetic offers from 20 publishers with the reference implementation, runs a query that returns 16 of them, and forms a decision view of the three cheapest new black offers. It counts the size of what a model would receive, using two publicly available tokenizers as proxies. The tokenizers of the models an agent actually uses may count differently.

The CSV row holds the same data as the JSON rows and converts back to it without loss. The decision view holds less: the runtime filtered and ranked before the model saw anything. These numbers say nothing about whether a model decides correctly with the smaller input. That requires task-level tests on named models, which have not been done.

ul.li: Is ADDP needed as a protocol, or should the feed rules, the query semantics and the runtime profile become profiles of UCP, ARD and OAuth?

Execution bindings for protocols in real use: an ACP binding needs an extension that lets the merchant reject a completion whose total differs from the one the runtime checked; a binding that uses AP2 needs a mapping from an intent to open mandates and a commerce protocol that provides requirements 2 and 3 of .
Whether a runtime should also bootstrap from ARD catalogs, agent.json files or UCP profiles, and how an index advertises itself in ARD registries.
How new resource and operation profiles are added without a new protocol version, and whether profiles and error codes need IANA registries .
Signed feeds, so that an index can pass on a publisher's records and a client can verify them without contacting the publisher.
Hosting a manifest or feed on another origin, as needed by content delivery networks and platforms that host many shops.
Predicates for location, shipping destination and dates, and a semantic search mode with defined behaviour.
Bindings for real checkout and payment protocols, and whether any of them meets today.
Task-level measurements of the model views on named models.
